title: Perform animal production and health care practices of cows and bulls

lessons.title: Production practices for cows and bulls
lessons.html:
Practical production tasks

In this practical module you carry out and supervise the routines that keep cows producing and breeding, and bulls working safely and effectively.

Managing cows through the cycle

  • Grouping: keep fresh cows, high producers, late lactation cows and dry cows in groups fed and managed for their stage.
  • Drying off: dry off cows on the date set by the herd plan, using the dry cow protocol the vet has prescribed, including any teat sealant or dry cow therapy; record and mark dry cows clearly.
  • Transition care: move close-up cows to the transition group on time; observe them several times a day for calving and early signs of milk fever or other problems.
  • Fresh cow checks: in the first days after calving check appetite, temperature, udder, uterine discharge and dung; report abnormal findings.
  • Body condition scoring: score at set stages and record; report cows that lose too much condition.

Reproduction tasks

  1. Observe for heat at set times each day and record heats with cow number and time.
  2. Use tail paint, chalk or activity data as the farm does; repaint as needed.
  3. Present cows for AI at the right time according to the farm's AM-PM rule or protocol.
  4. Record inseminations with sire and inseminator.
  5. Prepare cows for vet pregnancy checks: list of cows, records ready, crush and handling facilities safe.

Bull management

  • Keep bulls in sound condition, not too fat or thin, with good feet and legs.
  • Ask the vet to test bulls for breeding soundness and for venereal diseases as recommended before the breeding season.
  • Rotate or rest bulls according to the breeding plan.
  • Record which bull ran with which group and when.

Bull safety

Dairy bulls are among the most dangerous animals on a farm. Never turn your back on a bull, never enter a bull camp or pen alone, use proper bull handling facilities and escape routes, and never treat a calm bull as safe.

lessons.title: Health care practices for the herd
lessons.html:
Daily health observation

Watch cows at milking, at feeding and in camps. Use the parlour to check udders, milk, legs and attitude every day. Report cows that are off feed, lame, dull, have abnormal milk or a sudden drop in yield.

Common conditions and practical responses

ConditionSignsPractical response
Clinical mastitisClots, watery milk, hard swollen quarter, feverMark cow, milk separately, treat per vet protocol, record, withhold milk
Subclinical mastitisHigh cell count, positive CMTCMT test quarters, discuss with vet
Milk feverCow wobbly or down near calving, cold earsEmergency: call supervisor or vet; treat per protocol
LamenessLimping, arched back, short stridesLift and inspect foot, trained hoof trimmer or vet; footbath programme
Retained afterbirth, metritisMembranes hanging, foul discharge, feverReport to vet; do not pull membranes
Tick-borne diseaseHigh fever, anaemia, weaknessCall vet; follow tick control plan

Treating cows correctly

  1. Confirm the cow and the treatment with the supervisor or vet instruction.
  2. Use the correct product, dose, route and site.
  3. Use clean equipment; dispose of needles in the sharps container.
  4. Mark the cow clearly as treated.
  5. Record treatment, dose, date, person and milk and meat withdrawal end dates.
  6. Keep treated cows' milk out of the bulk tank until withdrawal ends; test if the farm requires.

Controlled diseases and herd health plan

Follow the herd health plan drawn up with the vet, including testing and vaccination required under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, such as brucellosis and tuberculosis testing as applicable. Keep certificates on file. Quarantine bought-in animals and keep movement records.

Hoof care and comfort

Maintain walkways free of stones, manage mud around troughs and gates, use footbaths as scheduled, and arrange routine hoof trimming.

Personal safety and hygiene

Stand to the side of cows, use crushes correctly, wear gloves for calvings, afterbirths and treatments, and wash hands. Brucellosis and TB can infect people.

Key points

  • Manage cows in groups by stage and follow dry-off and transition protocols.
  • Detect heats accurately and record inseminations.
  • Test bulls for breeding soundness; never work alone with bulls.
  • Respond to mastitis, milk fever, lameness and metritis by protocol.
  • Mark and record treated cows and protect the bulk tank.

quiz.question: What should be done before the breeding season for bulls?

options.text: Breeding soundness and disease testing by the vet
Fatten them as much as possible
Keep them indoors for a month

quiz.question: A cow has a hard, swollen quarter and clots in the milk. What should you do?

options.text: Milk her into the bulk tank
Mark her, milk separately and treat per the vet protocol

quiz.question: Membranes are hanging from a cow after calving. What is correct?

options.text: Report to the vet and do not pull membranes

quiz.question: Which condition typically shows as a wobbly or downer cow near calving with cold ears?
A calm bull can be treated as safe.
Dry cows should be clearly marked and recorded.
